court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: Under the 1920 amendment barring summary proceedings to recover possession of property occupied for dwelling purposes, the statute protects a tenant who has sublet floors of a private house to a number of subtenants for dwelling use, and the landlord may not evict on the theory that the tenant "made a business" of subletting furnished apartments.

quotes.text: The respondent urges that as between the landlords and this particular tenant the tenant “made a business ” of subletting furnished apartments. The statute does not, however, recognize the nice distinction thus sought to be superimposed upon it.
It seems to me to be perfectly clear that these premises fall within the description of the” statute quoted, and that, therefore, summary proceedings will not lie.

notes: Court draws no legal distinction between a tenant sub-letting furnished apartments as a business and an ordinary dwelling tenant for purposes of statutory eviction protection; characterization left null because the court does not classify the arrangement as lease/license/lodging/innkeeping, only as within the statute's 'dwelling purposes' language.
Ordinary apartment lease holdover / use-and-occupation rent dispute under the 1920 housing laws; no lodging, boarding, or room-letting practice at issue.
Zoning certiorari case over a Board of Appeals variance permitting a business building in a residence district; no lodging/boarding issue.

holding_summary: Where a complaint alleges that a landlord is renting furnished rooms to lodgers and permitting overcrowding in violation of the Health Law and Tenement House Law, an injunction will not lie absent proof that the city departments charged with enforcing those laws have failed to perform their duty.

quotes.text: Plaintiffs further complained that the landlord is renting out furnished rooms to lodgers andi allowing them to occupy these rooms in such large numbers as to overcrowd the apartments, in consequence of which the health and safety of the plaintiffs are threatened, in contravention of the Health Law and the Tenement House Law.

Plaintiffs further complained that the landlord is renting out furnished rooms to lodgers andi allowing them to occupy these rooms in such large numbers as to overcrowd the apartments, in consequence of which the health and safety of the plaintiffs are threatened, in contravention of the Health Law and the Tenement House Law.

The manner of enforcing the Health Law or the Tenement House Law is prescribed by the statute itself. This court may not usurp the powers delegated by law to the various city departments having the enforcement of such laws in charge, in the absence of any proof of failure on the part of the public officials to properly perform their duty.

notes: Injunction denied on procedural/remedial grounds (adequate statutory enforcement channel), not on the merits of the lodging arrangement itself; marked adverse because the case situates letting of furnished rooms to lodgers within the Health Law/Tenement House Law police-power regulatory framework governing overcrowding.
Month-to-month apartment tenancy notice-to-quit dispute (Sylvester Flats); ordinary whole-apartment rental, not lodging/boarding or short-term room letting.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: The statutory protection against summary dispossession of property occupied for dwelling purposes applies only where the tenant himself occupies the premises for dwelling purposes; a lessee who lives elsewhere and instead sublets floors as apartments or operates the premises as a rooming house as a business venture for profit is not entitled to that protection.

quotes.text: The tenant as principal lessee either lets out the floors of the building as apartments to subtenants, or uses the premises for a rooming house.
This means that unless the tenant himself occupies the premises for dwelling purposes, he is not entitled to the protection of the statute.

This tenant has not been subjected to oppression by fear of being deprived of a home. On the contrary, the tenant is housed elsewhere, and is engaged in a business venture in these premises to make money.

notes: Court expressly distinguishes a commercial rooming-house/subletting business from a genuine dwelling occupant, denying the statutory shield to the former.
Copyright dispute over rights to a musical composition ('Crazy Blues'); wholly unrelated to lodging/letting of dwellings.
Restrictive-covenant dispute over whether a private garage falls within a 'barn or private stable' restriction; no lodging/letting issue.

holding_summary: A tenant who long occupied leased premises consisting of a store used for his own business and rear rooms used for dwelling may not be dispossessed under the emergency housing law from any part of the premises merely because part is used for business, and subletting of a room for profit while retaining dwelling occupancy of the remainder is treated as merely incidental to, and does not defeat, the statutory dwelling-purposes protection.

quotes.text: Such a subletting is merely incidental to the occupancy by the tenant of the entire premises for dwelling purposes.

There is nothing in the act either express or by implication that would permit the court to regulate or fix the extent of the occupancy or possession to which the tenant was entitled on October 1, 1920, or that permits the court to sever a room used for business purposes by consent under the original hiring from the remainder of the premises occupied for dwelling purposes.

notes: Characterization left null: the court addresses the scope of statutory 'dwelling purposes' protection over mixed business/dwelling premises rather than classifying a letting as lease/license/lodging/innkeeping; the doctrinally significant point is its treatment of a householder-tenant's profit subletting of rooms as an ordinary incident of dwelling occupancy (citing Jackson v. Grey and Howie v. McKenzie).
Divorce/domicile case; mother-in-law's 'rooming house' is mentioned only in passing as background, with no bearing on the legal character of lodging or its regulation.
